title: Peter's Confession and the Way of the Cross
summary: Pharisees and Sadducees demand a sign, and Jesus warns his disciples against their teaching, which he calls leaven. At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, and Jesus declares that on this rock he will build his church and gives Peter the keys of the kingdom. Jesus then begins to teach that he must suffer, die, and rise, rebukes Peter for resisting, and calls his followers to take up their cross.
story: This chapter is the hinge of Matthew's Gospel. Everything so far has raised the question of who Jesus is: the crowds guess, the leaders accuse, the disciples wonder. Now, far north of the crowds, Jesus asks the question directly and Peter answers it. The phrase “From that time on Jesus began” (verse 21) marks a turn, echoing 4:17, where Jesus began to preach. From here the Gospel moves toward Jerusalem and the cross. The disciples have learned who Jesus is; they must now learn what kind of Messiah he is, and Peter, who gets the first lesson right, gets the second one wrong in the same scene.
historical:
The Pharisees and Sadducees appear together as allies here, though they disagreed on much. The Sadducees were a party of priestly and aristocratic families centered on the temple in Jerusalem. They accepted only the written law as binding, rejected the Pharisees' oral traditions, and denied the resurrection of the dead (22:23). Their shared opposition to Jesus is the more striking for their differences. Verses 2 and 3, the sayings about reading the sky, are missing from some of the oldest Greek manuscripts, and scholars debate whether they were part of Matthew's original text.

Caesarea Philippi lay about twenty-five miles north of the Sea of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon, beside one of the springs that feed the Jordan. The site had long been known as Paneas for its cave shrine to the Greek god Pan. Herod the Great built a temple there in honor of Augustus, and his son Philip the tetrarch enlarged the town and renamed it Caesarea in the emperor's honor; it was called Philippi's Caesarea to distinguish it from the coastal Caesarea. It was a largely Gentile city, full of the symbols of pagan religion and imperial power, and the confession of Jesus as Christ and Son of the living God rings out against that background. The parallel accounts are Mark 8:27-9:1 and Luke 9:18-27; only Matthew records Jesus' words to Peter in verses 17 to 19.
cultural:
Leaven, a lump of fermented dough kept from one batch to start the next, works invisibly through the whole loaf, and it was often an image of corrupting influence (as in 1 Corinthians 5:6-8). Here it stands for the teaching of the religious leaders. Simon son of Jonah uses the Aramaic form Bar-Jonah, son of Jonah; John 1:42 calls his father John, and the names may be variant forms. The name Peter translates the Aramaic Kepha (Cephas), which means rock or stone.

Keys in the ancient world belonged to a steward who managed a household on the master's behalf. Isaiah 22:22 describes God giving Eliakim, the steward of David's palace, the key of the house of David, so that what he opens no one shuts. Binding and loosing were terms later used by Jewish teachers for forbidding and permitting under the law, and also for imposing or lifting a ban from the community. The gates of Hades would suggest the realm of the dead and the power of death; Hades is the Greek name for the underworld, corresponding to the Hebrew Sheol. To take up a cross meant, for any first-century hearer, the walk of a condemned man to his execution.
literary: The chapter has two parts, turning on verse 21. In the first (verses 1 to 20), Jesus refuses the leaders a sign, corrects the disciples' literal misunderstanding about bread, and receives Peter's confession. In the second (verses 21 to 28), he predicts his passion for the first time, and the scene with Peter is built as a mirror of the first: blessed by the Father in verse 17, Peter is called Satan in verse 23; the rock on which the church is built becomes a stumbling stone (skandalon); his first insight came from God, his objection from human thinking. The chapter ends with a saying about some who will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom, which many interpreters connect with the transfiguration that immediately follows in chapter 17, while others connect it with the resurrection or with the judgment on Jerusalem.

outline.t: The leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees
Jesus predicts his death; Peter rebuked

doctrines.note: Peter's confession states the heart of the Gospel's claim: Jesus is the Christ, the anointed king Israel awaited, and the Son of the living God. Jesus accepts the confession but immediately redefines messiahship around suffering, death, and resurrection.

This is the first use of the word church in the Gospels. Jesus speaks of it as his own (“My church”), built by him, and promises that the power of death will not prevail against it. How Peter relates to its foundation is a question Christians answer differently, discussed below.

Jesus says he must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, and be raised. The word must (dei) expresses divine necessity: the cross is not an accident or a defeat but the path God has set, and resisting it is thinking the things of men.
Peter's confession did not come from flesh and blood but was revealed by the Father. Knowing who Jesus is remains God's gift, as in 11:25-27.

words.note: Petra, rock, a mass of bedrock. Jesus says “you are Peter” (Petros, a masculine form of the same word, used as a name) and then says that on this petra, this rock, “I will build My church.” In Aramaic, the language Jesus likely spoke, the same word kepha would stand in both places. What the rock refers to is the chapter's most debated question.

Ekklesia, assembly or church. In Greek cities it meant a gathering of citizens; in the Greek Old Testament it often translates the Hebrew qahal, the assembly of Israel gathered before God. Matthew is the only Gospel to use the word, here and in 18:17. Jesus speaks of forming a new assembly of God's people around himself.

Kleis, key. Keys symbolize authority to open and close, admit and exclude, as with the steward in Isaiah 22:22. Jesus later rebukes scribes and Pharisees for shutting the kingdom in people's faces (23:13), which suggests the keys concern opening the way in through the message of the kingdom.

Aparneomai, to deny or disown. To deny oneself in verse 24 is not to reject one's worth but to refuse self as the final master. The same verb describes Peter's denial of Jesus in 26:34, 35, and 75, where he says three times that he does not know him.

christ: The chapter is the Gospel's clearest statement of who Jesus is and what he has come to do. He is the Christ, the Son of the living God, and he is the builder and owner of the church. He is also the Son of Man who must suffer, die, and on the third day be raised, and who will come in his Father's glory to judge. Jesus holds together what Peter cannot: the glory of Daniel 7's Son of Man and the suffering of Isaiah 53's Servant. The call to take up the cross makes his road the road of his followers, and the saying that whoever loses his life for his sake will find it is the pattern of his death and resurrection applied to them. The demand for a sign is answered again with Jonah, whose three days point to the resurrection that Jesus now begins to predict plainly.

hard.q: What is the rock on which Jesus builds his church, and what authority did he give Peter?
hard.a:
Christians have read verses 18 and 19 in several ways. The Catholic Church teaches that the rock is Peter himself, chosen as the visible foundation and chief shepherd of the church, and that the keys and the ministry they signify pass to his successors as bishops of Rome. On this view the passage grounds the papacy: Peter receives a unique office, and the promise that the gates of Hades will not prevail assures the church's continuity through that office.

The Orthodox churches honor Peter as first among the apostles, and many Orthodox writers emphasize that the rock is Peter's confession of faith, or Peter as the one who confesses it. They hold that the authority of the keys belongs to the whole episcopate, all bishops in apostolic succession who hold the same faith, and they reject the claim that the bishop of Rome has universal jurisdiction over the church. Many Protestants, following Reformers such as Luther and Calvin, have taken the rock to be Peter's confession or Christ himself, noting that Paul calls Christ the only foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11). Many Protestant scholars today agree that the wordplay points to Peter as a person, the foundational apostle who led the early church (as in Acts 2 and 10), while holding that nothing in the text speaks of successors.

All three traditions agree that Christ is the builder and owner of the church, that Peter held a real leading role among the apostles, and that the authority to bind and loose, extended to the disciples in 18:18, concerns the message and discipline of the kingdom. Where they differ is whether and how Peter's role continues. Early Christian writers themselves read the rock in more than one way; Augustine, for instance, at different times took it as Peter and as Christ and left readers to judge. This is a question on which faithful Christians remain divided.

questions: Jesus asks, “Who do you say I am?” How would you answer in your own words, and how has your answer changed over time?
Peter could confess Jesus as Christ and still resist a suffering Messiah. Where do you want Jesus' power without his cross?
What does it mean for you, concretely, to deny yourself and take up your cross this week?
